system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 12 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 60-85 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2201-02-20 00:26:00 to 2201-03-03 14:30:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: Mr. Thompson was admitted with right-sided testicular pain and swelling, presenting with fever and leukocytosis. He was diagnosed with febrile epididymo-orchitis, supported by scrotal ultrasound showing right testicular inflammation and a complex hydrocele likely representing a pyocele. He was treated with IV cefepime initially, with improvement in symptoms and white blood cell count. Urine cultures grew E. coli resistant to ciprofloxacin and Bactrim, and pan-sensitive Proteus, both sensitive to cephalosporins. He remained afebrile, and his renal function and potassium normalized. He was discharged on oral cefpodoxime for a 14-day course, with updated warfarin dosing and instructions to follow up with his urologist and primary care provider. His chronic conditions, including heart failure, diabetes, cirrhosis, and anticoagulation, were managed without complication.
problems: Urinary tract infection, site not specified
Chronic combined systolic and diastolic heart failure
Diabetes mellitus without mention of complication, type II or unspecified type, not stated as uncontrolled
Cirrhosis of liver without mention of alcohol
Other and unspecified Escherichia coli [E. coli]
Proteus (mirabilis) (morganii) infection in conditions classified elsewhere and of unspecified site
Chronic airway obstruction, not elsewhere classified
Coronary atherosclerosis of unspecified type of vessel, native or graft
Automatic implantable cardiac defibrillator in situ
Personal history of transient ischemic attack (TIA), and cerebral infarction without residual deficits
Heart valve replaced by other means

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Mr. Thompson. I’m Dr. Lee, one of your hospital doctors. You were transferred here because of shortness of breath and low blood counts. Can you tell me more about how you’ve been feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, doctor. For the past few days, I’ve been getting winded just walking to the bathroom. I’ve also been more tired than usual. But no chest pain or cough.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Your blood work shows your hemoglobin is quite low—6.5—so we think you’ve been losing blood slowly, likely from your GI tract. That’s why you’re so tired and short of breath.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh… I didn’t notice any black stools or vomiting blood. Is that possible?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, sometimes bleeding can be slow and not obvious. We’ve scheduled an EGD today—a scope of your stomach—to look for the cause.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. Thompson, the EGD is done. We found a 2.5 cm polyp in your stomach, near the opening to the small intestine. We took a biopsy, and the preliminary report suggests it may be cancerous.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Cancer? In my stomach? That’s… that’s a lot to take in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. It’s early stage—confined to the polyp—and we didn’t see anything else suspicious. The good news is we can remove it completely with another procedure called EMR.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that cure it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s very likely, especially since it hasn’t spread. We’ll confirm with the final pathology and do a CT scan to be sure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re holding your warfarin for now because of the planned procedure. We’ve started a heparin drip to protect your heart valve while you’re not on Coumadin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on warfarin for years. Is it safe to stop it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s safe for a short time when we replace it with heparin. Your INR goal is 2.0–2.5 because of your liver condition, so we’ll watch that closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your EMR was successful. The entire mass was removed. You’ll need to stay on a proton-pump inhibitor like pantoprazole to help it heal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. Any pain or bleeding risk after the procedure?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Some mild discomfort is normal. We’ll monitor your blood counts and keep you on clear liquids today. No heavy lifting or straining.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did an X-ray tonight because you had some belly pain. Good news—no free air, so no perforation. Just some normal post-procedure changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks, doctor. I was worried about that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your hemoglobin is stable at 7.6 now—still low, but not dropping. We’re not giving a transfusion unless it falls further.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that safe with my heart condition?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, because you’re not actively bleeding and your heart is stable. We’re watching closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re pausing your torsemide for now. Your kidney function dipped a bit after the CT contrast, so we’re being cautious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I usually take that for swelling. Should I be worried about fluid buildup?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. Your lungs are clear, and you’re not retaining much fluid. We’ll restart it once your creatinine improves.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The CT scan results are back. No signs of cancer spread—no tumors in your chest, abdomen, or pelvis. That’s excellent news.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s just in the stomach and we got it all out?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. The pathology confirmed it was a poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma, but caught early. You’ll follow up with oncology as an outpatient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do I need chemotherapy?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s for the oncology team to decide. Given the early stage, it may not be needed. They’ll review everything at your appointment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your INR is now 2.5, back in the safe range. We’ve restarted your warfarin and stopped the heparin drip.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I was nervous about my valve without the blood thinner.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Completely understandable. You’re now protected again. We’ve adjusted your warfarin schedule slightly to keep your INR stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your liver function is stable. The CT confirmed cirrhosis, but no complications like varices or fluid. Your MELD score is 19, which is moderate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I see a liver specialist?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve scheduled a follow-up with hepatology. They’ll monitor your liver and discuss any needed interventions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your breathing has improved. The BNP was high when you arrived, and your chest X-ray showed some fluid, but now your lungs are clear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I can walk to the end of the hall now without stopping. That’s progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Definitely. We’ll keep managing your heart failure with medications, just not the diuretic until your kidney function is back to baseline.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The oncology team visited today. They agree—no immediate chemo needed. Just close monitoring and follow-up endoscopies.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a huge weight off my shoulders.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep you on pantoprazole twice daily until your GI doctor says otherwise. It helps the stomach heal and reduces cancer recurrence risk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs this morning look good. Hemoglobin holding at 7.6, creatinine down to 1.3, and INR at 2.5. We’re planning for discharge tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. What do I need to do when I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take all your medications, especially warfarin and pantoprazole. Don’t restart torsemide—that’s on hold until your primary doctor clears it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the follow-up tests?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—get a CBC, basic metabolic panel, and INR done in a few days. Fax the results to your primary care doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll follow up with your primary care provider, oncology, and hepatology. Make sure to mention any black stools, vomiting, or severe belly pain right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And if I feel short of breath again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call your doctor or come in. But you’re much stronger now, and your heart function is stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Mr. Thompson. You’re cleared for discharge. Your condition is stable, and all critical issues are addressed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor. I appreciate everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Remember—no torsemide, take pantoprazole twice daily, and keep all your follow-up appointments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the warfarin schedule changed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—now 5 mg five times a week and 7.5 mg twice a week. We updated your prescription. Your INR target remains 2.0 to 2.5.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And the stomach cancer—how often do I need checkups?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Oncology will decide, but likely every few months initially. They may repeat an EGD in 6 months to ensure no recurrence.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make sure to go. Anything else I should watch for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Signs of bleeding—black stools, dizziness, or weakness. Also, fever or severe abdominal pain. Otherwise, focus on rest and recovery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you again for explaining everything so clearly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check before you leave—your weight is 82.6 kg, down from admission. That suggests you’ve lost some fluid, which is good for your heart.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel lighter, actually.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And your oxygen level is 97% on room air—excellent. Lungs are clear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I can breathe so much better now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re glad. Keep using your inhalers for your COPD as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t needed the albuterol as much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a sign your overall condition is improving. Keep up the good work.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—my diabetes meds were held in the hospital. Should I restart them?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve restarted metformin and glipizide. Watch your blood sugar, especially since your diet is back to normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I usually check it twice a day. I’ll keep doing that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. And if you have any questions, call the clinic. We’re here to help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate that. I feel ready to go home now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re confident you’ll do well. Take it easy for the next week or two.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I plan to. No gardening or heavy lifting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Let your body heal. And congratulations on getting through this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor. Really.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. Take care, Mr. Thompson.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will bring your discharge papers and prescriptions shortly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll wait for her.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll also send a summary to your primary care doctor and specialists.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I want them all on the same page.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They will be. Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, Mr. Thompson.

summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. Thompson was admitted for evaluation of progressive dyspnea and symptomatic anemia with hemoglobin of 6.5 g/dL. He was found to have a 2.5 cm gastric polyp in the incisura, which biopsy confirmed as poorly differentiated invasive adenocarcinoma. He underwent endoscopic mucosal resection (EMR) without complications. Staging CT showed no metastatic disease. His anticoagulation was managed with heparin bridging during the procedure, and warfarin was resumed with INR 2.5 at discharge. Heart failure was managed conservatively, with temporary discontinuation of torsemide due to acute kidney injury from contrast. His cirrhosis was stable, and he was discharged home with plans for oncology, hepatology, and primary care follow-up, along with outpatient lab monitoring.
